context.text: First — where does your plan live today?
answers: In a written document the board approved.
In a slide, a page, or a set of goals we've written down.
In conversations — we know what we're about, but it isn't written down.
Honestly, we're not sure we have one.
reflect: You told us your plan lives in a document the board approved.
You told us your plan lives in a page or a set of written goals.
You told us your plan lives in conversation rather than on paper — which is where most of the organisations we work with begin.
You told us you're not sure you have a plan — which is a more honest starting point than most.

questions.text: If you stopped three people in the hallway — a board member, a manager, someone on the front line — and asked why the organisation is heading where it's heading, what would you hear?
answers: The same one or two sentences, in their own words.
The same idea in different words; someone might need a moment.
The board member could say it; the other two would guess.
A list of goals — or a friendly shrug.

questions.text: Think of one thing the organisation has decided to do this year — a project, a change, a push. Who owns it?
answers: One named person, and they'd tell you so themselves.
A named person on paper; in practice it's shared.
A team, or a committee.
It's "all of us" — which usually means no one in particular.

questions.text: What has to happen in the next ninety days for that to move — and by when?
answers: We could tell you the first steps and their dates; they're on people's calendars.
We know the steps; the dates are "this year".
We know the direction, not the steps.
We haven't broken it down that far yet.

questions.text: How will you know it's working — and do you know where you started?
answers: We have measures with a starting number, a target, and the steps between.
We have targets; starting numbers for some.
We'd know it when we saw it.
We haven't put numbers to it — it's an aim.

questions.text: When did the board last talk about where the organisation is going — not the budget, the direction?
answers: Last quarter, and it looked like the quarter before.
Once this year, in whatever form was to hand.
When the plan — or the goals — were approved.
It doesn't really come up as its own conversation.

questions.text: Some of what the direction rests on you know, and some you believe. Could you point to which is which?
answers: Yes — the facts have sources, the assumptions are written down, and someone's checking them.
We know the difference in our heads; it isn't written down.
We treat it all as known.
We haven't asked ourselves that.

questions.text: Who was asked what they needed before the direction was set — and who was on the list and never heard from?
answers: We can name who was asked, how many answered, and who we missed.
We asked widely; we couldn't tell you the response rate.
Leadership and the board.
Mostly the people who set it.

questions.text: What did you decide not to do — and does the board know why?
answers: The board saw the paths we didn't take, and why.
We weighed options; the board saw the recommendation.
There was one obvious path, so we took it.
We haven't ruled anything out — which may be the problem.

questions.text: When did someone in leadership last sit down with a member or customer nobody in the room already knew?
answers: This quarter — it's a habit with a name.
This year, informally.
We have survey numbers.
We know our members; we haven't felt the need.

questions.text: If the one person who holds a key process together left this month, what happens?
answers: We've named who those people are, and there's a plan for each.
We know who they are; nothing's written down.
We'd manage — we always have.
I'd rather not think about it.

bands.label: Rooted
bands.text: Whatever form your plan takes, it's alive: people can say why, the work has owners and dates, and the board sees the same picture each quarter. That's rarer than you'd think. What we'd look at with you is the ground under it — which of the things it rests on are still assumptions rather than facts, and who you haven't heard from lately. That's what carries a plan through a change of leadership, and it's usually a short piece of work.

bands.label: Taking hold
bands.text: There's a real direction here, and parts of it are working. Where things in this band tend to go quiet is between the intention and the calendar: work that belongs to a team rather than a person, measures without a starting number, a board that saw it once. None of that is hard to fix — and if your plan lives mostly in conversation, writing those few things down is most of the job. We'd start with owners and first moves, ninety days by date, and build the quarterly look-back around them.

bands.label: Still underground
bands.text: The direction is in the soil more than above it — and that's true whether it's a document nobody opens or a shared understanding nobody has written down. Most of the organisations we're proudest of working with started here. It isn't a strategy problem so much as a ground problem: the why hasn't been said out loud together, so nothing beneath it connects. We'd start at the root — a short conversation about what the organisation is truly for — before writing anything. It takes less time than people fear, and it usually goes better than people expect.
